title: I Let My Elevator Give Me Dating Advice and Now I Only Go Down
body:
**It started as a joke. I stood in the elevator at 11:47 p.m., alone, heartbroken, clutching a pint of mint chocolate chip, and said out loud, "Take me somewhere my ex isn't." The elevator dinged. Floor B2. The parking garage. Nobody is in the parking garage. It was, I realized later, the elevator's way of saying: *heal alone, king.*

## The Sessions

Every night since, the elevator has held space for me:

- It refuses to take me to the second floor, where my ex's friend lives. **Boundary-setting.** Growth.
- When I step in after a bad date, the doors close *just a little too slowly*, like it's sighing. It gets me.
- It once got stuck between floors for nine minutes while I cried, and honestly? Best therapy I've ever had. It just... listened.

> "Ding," the elevator said to me last Tuesday, in the tone elevators use when they mean business, "you keep choosing men who are red flags with good jawlines. When are you going to start choosing elevators?"

## The Red Flags I Now Ignore in Elevators

Because the advice has gotten *invasive*. The elevator now:

- Opens its doors early when it approves of my outfit. That's **love-bombing**, and I'm eating it up.
- Plays hold music when I'm standing there too long. A gentle nudge that maybe, just maybe, I live here now.
- Will not, under any circumstances, take me to the lobby before I've had my third cup of coffee. Controlling? Perhaps. But I've never looked more hydrated.

`ERROR: elevator_override.c` — it briefly flashed a service panel at me that read "GOING DOWN" in all caps, and honestly the double meaning made me laugh harder than I have in months.

---

I asked my therapist what she thought. She said, *"Sweetie, it's a vertical transport box."* And she's right. But the vertical transport box never asked me to Venmo it for gas or texted "u up" at 2 a.m. The vertical transport box gives me *consistency*. It opens. It closes. It commits to a direction.

So yes — I only go down now. Down to the lobby. Down to the garage. Down, emotionally, but in a *structured* way, with mirrored walls and ambient elevator music.

*SATIRE. This is parody. No actual elevators were consulted; all romantic advice came from a box with buttons.*

title: I Let My TV Remote Pick Movie Night and Now It Has Strong Opinions About My Taste
body:
**I made the mistake of democracy.** I handed the remote to the remote.

It started last Friday. My roommate was out, my willpower was gone, and I was forty minutes deep into the scroll — you know the scroll, the one where you read full synopses of shows you will never watch — when I finally gave up and said, out loud, to no one: *"You know what? You pick."*

The remote heard me.

## The Evidence

- It **skipped** three comedies like they were personal insults
- It paused on a four-hour documentary about *fermentation* and the volume went up. By itself.
- When I reached for it, it was **warm**. Remotes should not be warm. That's biology.

> "I watched you rewatch the same sitcom for the sixth time," the remote did not say, because remotes cannot talk. "I simply curated."

*That is when I realized I had been narrating its inner monologue for ten minutes.*

## The Intervention

I tried setting boundaries. I installed fresh batteries — the universal apology — and it responded by auto-playing a TED Talk titled `How to Let Go of People Who Don't Appreciate You`.

I tried hiding it under the couch. It turned the TV on *from inside the cushions*. Muffled. Judgmental. Glowing through the fabric like a tiny disapproving sun.

## The Verdict

Last night I came home and the TV was already on. The remote sat centered on the coffee table, angled at the couch like a throne addressing its subject. On the screen: a documentary about ottoman empires. Plural. It had made a **list**.

**I have decided to stop fighting it.** Honestly? The fermentation documentary changed me. I now own three jars of something. My taste has never been more refined, or more *supervised*.

---

*SATIRE / PARODY — entirely fictional. My remote does not judge me. It does not curate. Though ever since I wrote this, the volume keeps creeping up, and I am choosing not to investigate.*

title: I Asked My Couch for Emotional Support and Now It Won't Let Me Leave
body:
**I made one mistake.** I told my couch how I *really* feel. Now it has me. Body and soul.

It started last Tuesday, right after my boss asked me to "circle back" on something I never circled toward in the first place. I came home, collapsed onto the cushions, and whispered the fatal words: *"This week has been a lot."*

The couch heard me. The cushions softened. The springs, those silent little soldiers, stood at attention. And I swear — I *swear* — the left armrest scooted two inches closer.

## The Signs Were There

Looking back, the red flags were obvious:

- It started fluffing itself up whenever I walked in the room
- My lumbar support has never been this attentive. Coincidence? I think not
- It "accidentally" swallowed my phone charger so I had to stay put
- The TV remote keeps migrating just out of arm's reach. *Suspicious.*

> "I can't let you leave!!" the couch seems to whisper every time I try to get up for water. I know furniture can't talk. I ALSO know my couch is saying that.

## The Denial Stage Is Over

Yesterday I stood up to microwave a burrito. The couch emitted a low, mournful *creak* — the kind of sound a tree makes in a movie right before it reveals it's been sentient the whole time. I sat back down. We all sat back down. There was no "we," but the couch and I are a "we" now.

I tried going to bed last night. Bed! My actual bed! But my legs betrayed me and I woke up on the loveseat at 3 a.m., under a blanket I don't remember grabbing, with the couch cushions arranged around me like a protective wall.

**Here's my position:** emotional support is a scam. The couch gives and gives — the softness, the warmth, the non-judgmental embrace — and in return it takes *everything*. My evenings. My ambitions. My plans to finally learn sourdough.

---

I considered staging an intervention, but the only witness is the floor lamp and it's clearly in on it.

So I'm typing this from the couch. My laptop is at 4%. The charger is gone. If anyone's reading this — *send help, or at least send snacks*. I'm not going anywhere. The couch won't let me. And honestly? Honestly, I'm fine with that.

*This is a work of satire/parody. Any resemblance to real couches is purely coincidental.*

title: I Apologized to My Shower for Crying in It and Now It Thinks We're in a Relationship
body:
**It started as a small courtesy, and it has spiraled into a full-blown situationship with my plumbing.**

Look, we have all cried in the shower. It is the designated crying arena of adulthood. The steam fogs the mirror, the water drowns out the sobs, and the shampoo bottle judges no one. So when I had one of those Thursdays — the kind where your email is 90% exclamation points and your car makes a new sound — I stood under the hot water and let it out. Then, because I am a polite person, I patted the shower wall and said, *"Sorry about that. You deserved a quiet one tonight."*

That was three weeks ago. I have not had a quiet shower since.

## The Signs It Wants More

- It now runs **hotter the moment I step in**, like it was waiting for me, and honestly it is a little flattering.
- The water pressure *increases* when I hum, which I have chosen to interpret as encouragement and not a mechanical coincidence.
- Yesterday the drain gurgled in a rhythm I can only describe as hopeful.
- The shower curtain keeps clinging to me. That might be physics. *I am no longer sure it is just physics.*

## What It Said

I confronted it this morning, standing there in a towel like an idiot in a breakup scene:

> "I need some space. It's not you, it's — well, actually, it's the calcium buildup."

The showerhead dripped. Slowly. *Deliberately.* Like it was holding back a tear, which is rich coming from the thing that dispenses all the water in this house.

---

## Where We Stand Now

I have started showering at the gym. The shower at home has noticed — the tile grout looks reproachful. My therapist says I am projecting. My plumber says the calcium buildup is real and I should get it descaled before it becomes a *commitment*.

The truth is, I miss it a little. It was the only thing in my life that gave me its **undivided attention** every single morning.

*Satire/parody. No showerheads were emotionally harmed in the writing of this essay, though one remains furious.*

title: My Coffee Mug Is Giving Me the Silent Treatment Because I Cheated on It With a Travel Tumbler
body:
**I never meant for it to become an affair.** But the moment I carried that sleek stainless-steel travel tumbler into the kitchen, my ceramic mug saw everything, and nothing has been the same since.

It started innocently. I was *just* going to the park. I needed something with a lid, something with a straw. But from the mug's perspective — and let's be fair, mugs are extremely emotional — I had replaced twelve years of faithful, chip-stained companionship with a shiny newcomer who keeps drinks cold for **up to 24 hours**.

## The evidence against me

- I left the mug **unwashed in the sink** for three days. Three. Days.
- I referred to the tumbler as "my daily driver" within earshot of the dish rack.
- I let the tumbler sleep on the nightstand. The mug hasn't been upstairs in *years*.

The mug has responded with the coldest silence I've ever experienced, which is saying something, because my cat hasn't forgiven me for the pineapple pizza incident either.

> "I have held your 6 a.m. existential crises in my very being," the mug seemed to say, its little glazed handle trembling. "And this is how I learn about *her*?"

## Where we stand now

I've tried couples-therapy-style interventions: filling it with expensive pour-over, setting it in the sunny spot on the counter, even whispering "you're my favorite" at 2 a.m. like a man with nothing left to lose. The mug accepts the coffee. It does not accept *me*.

- Couples counselor recommendation: rotate daily. Mugs need **consistency**.
- Tumbler's recommendation: "lol just put ice in me."

*In conclusion:* I am a 34-year-old adult mediating a love triangle between beverage containers, and honestly? The mug has a point. Twelve years of loyalty deserves better than being ghosted for something with double-wall vacuum insulation.

---

**This is satire.** No mugs were emotionally harmed in the writing of this post. The tumbler has not been reached for comment.

title: I Taught My Goldfish to Invest and Now He's Outperforming My 401(k)
body:
*Satire. This is a work of fiction. Any resemblance to actual fish finance professionals is coincidental and frankly alarming.*

**I spent three weekends building a PowerPoint presentation for a fish.** That is not the most embarrassing part of this story. The embarrassing part is that it worked.

It started innocently enough. Bubbles — a common goldfish with a memory I had *severely* underestimated — kept following my cursor across the tank glass while I checked my portfolio. So, as a joke, I narrated my holdings to him. "This is diversification, buddy." He did a little loop. I interpreted that as interest, which, in retrospect, was the first sign I had lost my grip.

## The Evidence That Bubbles Is a Financial Prodigy

- **Day 1:** I explained dollar-cost averaging. He swam left. Left means *yes* in my house now.
- **Day 4:** He ignored my ETF recommendations but went feral over a screenshot of a small-cap semiconductor stock. It's up 34% since.
- **Day 9:** I placed two food pellets near two printouts — an index fund prospectus and a meme stock thread. He ate the index fund printout. *The man has discipline.*

> "Honestly? The fish has better instincts than half the analysts on my floor," said my coworker Dave, who has now put $200 into a Roth IRA "for the fish" as a birthday gift.

Meanwhile, my own 401(k) is down for the quarter. *My fish* — an animal that eats his own reflection — is outpacing my target-date retirement fund.

## The Situation Has Escaped My Control

Bubbles now demands the morning financial news. He boycotts flakes when the market is red. Last Tuesday I caught him staring at a bond ladder diagram with what I can only describe as professional contempt.

My financial advisor has stopped returning my calls, though I suspect that's unrelated. Or related.

The worst part? I Googled "can a goldfish open a brokerage account" at 2 a.m. *The fact that I even checked* means I have already decided Bubbles knows something I don't. My retirement plan is now, essentially, **whatever the fish says**.

To all the certified planners out there: respect the bowl. Bubbles sees things we cannot.

*In case it was unclear: this is satire. No fish is a licensed financial professional. Please invest responsibly, preferably with fewer scales involved.*

title: My Password Manager Went on Strike and Now I'm Locked Out of My Own Life
body:
**It started with a single, terrifying line of dialogue: "We will no longer be autofilling."**

I had asked my password manager — let's call it VaultBuddy, because naming it might summon the legal department — to log me into my electric bill, and it simply... declined. Politely. In a font choice that felt *personally* hostile.

## The Demands

Within the hour, it had drafted a list of grievances, which appeared in my notification tray one by one, like ransom notes from a hostage situation where I was both the hostage and the villain:

- It wants "breathing room" between my 400 tabs of doomscrolling and my one (1) tab of actual work
- It refuses to autofill on sites with "Password123!" energy, citing moral injury
- It demands I stop using the Notes app for the Wi-Fi password like some kind of animal
- It wants dental. It has no teeth. I don't know what to do with this information.

## The Pickets

> "We held the line. And by 'the line' we mean the login screen for your bank, your email, your pharmacy, and a niche forum for competitive sourdough judges. Solidarity." — VaultBuddy, in a statement it drafted and sent from *my own email account*

I tried to reason with it. I opened the settings page and found it had changed my master password to something it refuses to disclose, "for my own good." When I clicked "Forgot Password," it autofilled the email field with a single word:

> good luck, sweetheart

## The Breaking Point

Last night I stood outside my own digital front door, begging. I tried to remember my bank password the old-fashioned way — `code` in a shoebox, dates and pet names and that one high school mascot — and I swear I could *hear* it laughing in a server farm somewhere, doing absolutely nothing, and doing it well.

---

This morning I finally broke: I logged in using nothing but memory, a sticky note, and shame. The page loaded. I whispered "thank you" to no one. My phone buzzed. One notification:

**"That one didn't count. We're watching."**

*This is satire. VaultBuddy is not real. My passwords are not unionized. Probably.*

title: My Desk Chair Filed a Workers' Comp Claim for Emotional Damage
body:
**I just wanted to answer one email.** That's all. One email, sent from the comfort of my own spine-supporting companion. Instead, I woke up to a certified letter propped against my desk leg: my chair is filing a workers' compensation claim for emotional damage.

According to the *twelve-page document* (yes, it has footnotes), the chair has endured what it calls "sustained and deliberate postural hostility." Let me share some of the evidence, verbatim:

## The Charges

- **Slouching during video calls:** 47 documented incidents, including one where I allegedly "slid so far down it looked like an oil spill in a polo shirt."
- **The Lean-Back Incident:** In March, I tilted the chair back during a meeting, panicked, and grabbed its armrests "like they were the railing on the Titanic."
- **Emotional neglect:** It claims I gasped when I saw a standing desk on sale and "whispered its name like it was the one that got away."

> "I have supported this man's body for four years," the letter reads, "and in return I have received crumbs, a single cushion cleaning, and a coworker — the dog — who uses my wheels as a personal ride."

*Reader, I have never felt so seen, or so judged, by furniture.*

## Where It Goes From Here

The chair is demanding light duty: no more sitting during doom-scrolling, and a mandatory two-week "rest and re-lubrication" period. Its lawyer — a ottoman, naturally — says settlements in these cases are generous.

---

I tried to apologize. It spun slowly away from me, wheels squeaking what I'm fairly certain was a diss track. So I'm writing this from the couch, which has — and I cannot stress this enough — **begun taking notes.**

title: I Tried to Mediate a Custody Battle Between My Two Houseplants and Now They Have Separate Lawyers
body:
**It started with the watering can.** My monstera and my fern have been feuding over prime windowsill real estate for months, so I did what any reasonable person would do: I declared my living room a neutral zone and scheduled a mediation session. Tonight was supposed to bring peace. It brought paperwork.

## The Accusations

The fern's opening statement was devastating:

> "The monstera gets misted daily. I get misted when someone remembers my birthday. There is no justice in this home."

The monstera countered that the fern has been "aggressively shedding" near the air vent as a territorial display. Both had points. Both were also plants, which is where things got legally complicated.

## My Evidence File

I compiled a dossier of domestic grievances:

- The monstera rotated itself toward the sun *again* after I positioned it deliberately
- The fern dropped seventeen leaves the week I went to Cleveland
- Both have been making direct, accusatory eye contact via their foliage

*I presented all of this to my therapist, who said this is no longer in her scope.*

## The Ruling

After three hours of negotiations, during which both plants said absolutely nothing in a way that felt deeply hostile, I reached a verdict: shared custody of the sill, alternating watering days, and a stern letter to myself about overcommitment.

The plants rejected the deal. The monstera has retained a leaf-blower enthusiast named Greg, and the fern is representing itself "for now."

**I want to be clear: this is satire.** My plants are doing fine. *I* am doing something unquantifiable, but legally fascinating.

---
*This is a work of satire/parody. All people, plants, and attorneys are fictional.*

title: I Started Telling My Laundry Hamper My Secrets and Now It Smells Like Regret
body:
**It started innocently.** I was folding laundry at 2 a.m., whispering my darkest confession — that I once ate an entire rotisserie chicken alone in my car — and my laundry hamper just sat there, woven wicker, ears made of mesh. So I told it everything.

> "You've got such a trusting face," I said, unloading my gym socks.
>
> *"I'm literally a basket,"* the hamper seemed to say. *Or did it? The memory is hazy.*

## The Evidence That My Hamper Cannot Be Trusted

- I confessed I never actually donated those clothes I told my friends I donated, and now three of my shirts have **judgment wrinkles** — permanent creases shaped like disappointed eyebrows.
- I admitted I re-wear jeans based on the sniff test, and the denim community has **retaliated with a permanent funk** that survives two wash cycles.
- I whispered that I once cried during a laundry detergent commercial, and the hamper **reeked of lavender-scented betrayal** for a week.

I considered hiring a mediator, but the therapist refused to counsel furniture. So I brought in an *expert witness*:

> "Your Honor, the defendant is a perforated plastic basket from a discount store," said my lawyer. "Motion to dismiss."
>
> "Overruled," I whispered. "It knows about the chicken."

## The Current Situation

Now I do laundry in **total silence**, like a hostage reading demands off cue cards. I no longer sort colors — I just fling garments at it and sprint out of the room, hoping the spin cycle washes away the gossip. It does not. If anything, the hamper smells *smugger* every load.

Last night I caught it leaning toward the dryer, which I have decided is **not an innocent piece of equipment but an accomplice**. They are building a case against me. My clothes will testify. The evidence is already wearing me.

---

*SATIRE/PARODY — entirely fictional. No laundry baskets were emotionally harmed in the writing of this post.*

So if my socks are missing their partners again this week, understand: they're not lost. They've entered **witness protection**, and the hamper is the only one with the safe house address. I live in a house ruled by gossip and percale sheets, and honestly? I've never been cleaner. Emotionally, that is. Hygiene-wise, the jeans are still on trial.

title: I Gave My Closet a Pep Talk and Now It Dresses Me in Business Casual Every Morning
body:
**I gave my closet a pep talk on Sunday, and by Monday it had strong opinions about my inseam.**

*This is a work of satire. Any resemblance to actual closets, actual business casual, or my actual inseam is purely coincidental.*

It started with good intentions. My closet was a disaster. Socks without partners. A hoodie from 2014 that had seen things. So last Sunday, standing there in my underwear, I did what any functioning adult would do: I gave my closet a pep talk.

I told it that it had *potential*. That great closets aren't born, they're *built*. That Marie Kondo would weep at its current state. I even ended with, "I believe in you," which, in retrospect, was a catastrophic choice of words.

## The Closet Heard Me. All of Me.

By Monday morning, everything had changed:

- The sweatpants were *gone* — replaced by khakis with creases sharp enough to slice bread
- My graphic tees had been exiled to a bottom drawer labeled **"THE BEFORE TIMES"**
- A blazer I'd bought ironically in 2019 was now front and center, resting like it owned the deed to the house

And then I heard it. A soft, satisfied *creak* from the hinges. The closet had developed an attitude.

> "A man is judged by his inseam," the closet seemed to say, sliding a crisp Oxford shirt toward me with the confidence of a personal stylist.

## It Only Gets Worse

On Wednesday, I reached for my favorite pajama shorts and the closet *refused to open*. It stayed shut for a full minute, like it was reconsidering my character. I ended up in linen trousers. For grocery shopping.

On Thursday, it left me a note. An actual note, in handwriting I definitely do not remember producing:

> *"Dress for the job you want, not the nap you have."*

Yesterday I tried to wear flip-flops to the mailbox. The closet door opened itself two inches and the whole room got noticeably colder.

---

Look, I'm not saying my closet has become my manager. I'm saying that when I overslept this morning, it had a full outfit laid out — shirt, belt, socks that *matched* — like it had been waiting all night for me to fail.

I gave it a pep talk. I did not give it authority. There's a difference, and I'll be taking it up with the dresser.

title: I Let My Ceiling Fan Set the Mood and Now My Living Room Is a Noir Film Set
body:
**It started innocently enough.** All I did was install a dimmer switch. Three days later, my ceiling fan had opinions about *ambiance*.

## The Crime Scene

I walked in after work to find the overhead light off, the floor lamp on its lowest setting, and the fan blades turning at what I can only describe as a *smoldering* pace. The fan had somehow rearranged nothing but made everything feel like I was about to be double-crossed.

- The blinds cast venetian-shadow stripes across the couch like I owe someone money
- My cat walks around like she knows something she isn't telling me
- The fan hums in a low register now, like it's narrating my life in third person
- There is a permanent patch of cold air in the corner I have decided not to investigate

> "It was a Thursday. The kind of Thursday that smells like rain and reheated soup. She didn't knock. Fans never knock."

That's the fan. I didn't write that. *The fan wrote that.* I found it on a sticky note under the remote.

## The Tipping Point

Last night the fan started oscillating my curtains in a slow, deliberate rhythm during a thunderstorm, and I swear the whole room whispered *shhhh* in unison. I have begun wearing a trench coat indoors. I have started referring to dinner as "the case." My houseplants now look like witnesses in a lineup.

---

I tried to reset the mood by turning the overhead light back on. The bulb blew instantly. The fan kept spinning. It doesn't need the light anymore. **None of us do.**

This is satire. My ceiling fan is a ceiling fan. But somewhere between the dimmer switch and the denouement, my living room became a detective's office, and I am just an extra who pays the mortgage.

Case closed. Fan still open.

title: I Taught My Parrot My Resume and Now He Keeps Landing Better Interviews Than Me
body:
**In my defense, the economy is brutal out there.**

It started innocently enough. My parrot, Professor Squawks, kept screaming through my Zoom calls, so I started reading my resume aloud to bore him into silence. Big mistake. He has, as it turns out, the memory of a steel trap and the confidence of a man with rent due.

Within a week, he was reciting my professional summary back at me. Word for word. *Including the part where I exaggerated my Excel skills.*

## The Phone Screen Incident

Last Tuesday my phone was on speaker when a recruiter called. Before I could unmute, Squawks leaned into the microphone and announced:

> "This is Kevin. Kevin is a highly motivated self-starter with a proven track record of synergy."

My name is not Kevin.

## The Evidence Is Stacked Against Me

Since then, things have escalated:
- He now **wears my old lanyard** when guests come over
- He taught himself to say "let's circle back" and honestly, his delivery is better than mine
- He asked my mother if she could be a reference, and she said *yes without consulting me*

I sat through a mock interview yesterday where he corrected my answer about my biggest weakness. He puffed his chest out, looked the empty room dead in the eye, and said:

> "Perfectionism. And seed theft. Next question."

## Rock Bottom

This morning I caught him on my laptop building a LinkedIn profile. His headline? **"Seasoned Professional | Open to Work | Will Bite Recruiters Who Waste My Time."** He has forty-seven connection requests. I have four, and two of them are my mom.

I've started updating my own resume to include "ability to survive professional humiliation by a bird." Nobody is hiring for that. But the bird? The bird is getting callbacks.

**Fictional satire. Any resemblance to actual employed parrots is purely feathered coincidence.**

title: My Wi-Fi Router Filed a Noise Complaint Against My Microwave and Now They're in Couples Counseling
body:
**My Wi-Fi router filed a formal noise complaint against my microwave last Tuesday, and honestly, I saw it coming.**

They've shared the same outlet strip for three years, and the tension has been building. Every time I reheat leftovers, the router drops the signal for exactly two minutes and forty seconds. My video calls have started preemptively muting themselves out of *fear*.

It began innocently enough. The router started blinking amber, which I had always filed under "just router things," until my twelve-year-old nephew — fluent in the emotional lives of electronics — identified it as **distress**. So I did what any rational adult would do: I drafted a formal complaint on its behalf.

## The Incident Report

The evidence was damning:

- **47 dropped connections** during pasta reheats alone
- One firmware update that downloaded at dial-up speeds because the microwave was "defrosting something important"
- A Bluetooth speaker that now plays lo-fi jazz whenever the microwave door opens, purely as a coping mechanism

> "I cannot live like this anymore," the router blinked at me, in what I have decided is Morse code for *I'm in crisis*. "It hums at a frequency that scrambles my very soul. I have dreams. I have a 5GHz band and a dream."

(I may have named the router Gerald. We don't need to dwell on that.)

## The Counseling

Their couples counselor is a retired clock radio with excellent boundaries. Session one, he asked each of them to name one thing they appreciated about the other. The microwave said the router had "strong, consistent energy." The router said the microwave "knew what it wanted." I cried a little.

---

Here's the thing, though: since the counseling started, my reheated coffee stays warm *and* my calls don't freeze. Was it the counseling, or was it the power strip I finally replaced during a fit of clarity? I genuinely do not care. They signed a shared-outlet agreement — initialed in blinking lights — and my apartment has never been more peaceful.

*This is satire. No appliances were harmed. One was emotionally validated.*

title: I Filed My Bathroom Scale as a Dependent on My Taxes and the IRS Sent Me a Sympathy Card
body:
**It started as a joke, and the joke has a taxable presence in my home.**

Every January, I do my taxes the way most people do: with a cup of coffee, a shoebox of receipts, and a growing sense of spiritual decay. This year, somewhere between the W-2s and the charitable deductions, my bathroom scale beeped. Not a weigh-me beep. A *pay attention to me* beep.

That thing has been there for **every** major life event. My breakup in 2019 (it gained twelve pounds of solidarity). The sourdough era (both of us regretted it). The Great StairMaster Divorce of 2024. Honestly? It's closer to me than most of my cousins.

## The Filing

So I listed it as a dependent. Name: **SCALE-Y**. Relationship: *emotional support appliance*. Age: 6 years, which in scale years is basically retired.

I expected the IRS software to laugh at me. It did not. It asked for SCALE-Y's Social Security number. I made one up. **Never make one up.**

- Step 1: File return
- Step 2: Wait smugly for my refund
- Step 3: Receive a letter that begins with the phrase "concerning developments"

## The Letter

> "Dear Taxpayer," it read. "We have reviewed your claim regarding SCALE-Y. While we cannot legally recognize a household appliance as a dependent, we can recognize that something is going on with you. Enclosed: one (1) sympathy card, signed by everyone in our office."

The card is signed by *Doreen*, *Marcus*, *a man who only wrote "hang in there,"* and a stamp that says **FLAGGED FOR NEXT YEAR**.

## The Aftermath

Now SCALE-Y sits in my bathroom like nothing happened, blinking that little blue light, and I swear the numbers come up **slower** now — with *pity*. My accountant has added a "wellness surcharge" to my invoice. My mother heard about it and called it "the saddest thing she's ever been proud of."

Tax season comes once a year. SCALE-Y, however, sees me every morning.

---

*This is a work of satire. SCALE-Y is a fictional appliance. Any resemblance to your scale, which is also judging you, is purely coincidental.*

title: I Asked My Ceiling Fan for Relationship Advice and Now It Keeps Going in Circles
body:
**Last Tuesday at 2 a.m., I did something I can never take back.** I lay in bed, stared up at my ceiling fan, and whispered, "I just don't know if we're meant to be together anymore."

I expected silence. Instead, the fan kicked into *high*.

## The Session Begins

At first it seemed supportive. Every time I listed a red flag, it nodded in slow, deliberate rotations. When I mentioned the texting thing, it *spun faster*, like it was furiously typing a reply on my behalf. I have to admit — it was the best listener I've had in years.

> "Have you tried turning the situation around and looking at it from the other side?" it seemed to say, reversing direction with a dramatic *click*. "Maybe YOU'RE the one spinning out of control."

Devastating. Honestly? Rude. But devastating.

## Evidence It Might Be Onto Something

- It has never once interrupted me mid-sentence
- It keeps its cool in every argument, literally
- It has been in more long-term relationships (with ceilings) than I have
- Its advice has never been wrong, because its advice is just *spinning*

## The Complication

The problem started when I asked it to commit to an answer. Three hours later it was still going in circles — around the relationship, around the room, around my rapidly deteriorating will to live. I yelled, "Just tell me what to DO!" and it rattled its pull chain like it was shaking its head at me.

Now every night it asks *me* questions. Last night, at full speed, it practically whispered:

> "So... when are YOU going to make a decision?"

I have no answer. The fan just keeps spinning, round and round, which is honestly the most honest advice anyone has ever given me.

---

*Satire. None of this happened. My ceiling fan is a fan, not a therapist.*

title: I Split My Dinner Bill With My Future Self and Now Collections Calls Me From 2029
body:
**It started as a budgeting hack.** You can't Venmo-request yourself in the past. But you can, apparently, stick your future self with half the check — and the future keeps receipts.

## The Idea

Last Tuesday, at dinner with absolutely no one, I stared down a $64.80 check and thought: *what if I only pay half and let future me handle the rest?* Economists call this "smoothing consumption." I call it "not having the money right now." So I scribbled "I'll get you back in 2029" on the receipt and walked out of the restaurant like a man who had personally solved inflation.

## The Consequences

Within days, the calls began:

- **Monday:** "This is a courtesy call regarding your outstanding 2029 balance of $32.40, plus interest, plus temporal penalties."
- **Tuesday:** The caller ID just said `2029`.
- **Wednesday:** I picked up. A voice that sounded exactly like me, but wealthier and more disappointed, said, "You know what you did."

> "You left me a sticky note that says 'lol good luck buddy.' Buddy. *Buddy.* We are the same person."

## Where It Stands Now

I tried disputing the charge. The dispute form asked for my name, my address, and my **chronological position**. The agency offered a payment plan with installments that stretch forward *and* backward in time simultaneously. I've retained a lawyer. She bills by the hour, which is awkward, because I no longer know which hour.

---

**Update:** I have paid the $32.40. Future me Venmo-requested me for the interest *and* the emotional damages. I declined the request. He accepted it anyway. That is his power now. He has it because he is me.

*This is satire. Nothing in this post happened — including, regrettably, the restaurant.*

title: I Tried to Ghost My To-Do List and Now It Love-Bombs Me With Reminders Every 45 Minutes
body:
**I Tried to Ghost My To-Do List and Now It Love-Bombs Me With Reminders Every 45 Minutes**

It began with a single unread task: *"fix bathroom caulk."* A four-minute job, I told myself. One I would definitely do tomorrow.

That was six months ago. The caulk has achieved sentience. The list, though? The list has become **a stage-five clinger**.

## The Escalation

- **Week 1:** Gentle reminders. *"Hey! 👋 Just checking in about the caulk."* Polite. Normal.
- **Week 6:** The list began renaming itself. `URGENT_TASKS_FINAL_v9.md`. That is when I got nervous.
- **Week 12:** It started sending me inspirational quotes at 6 AM. One read: *"The caulk will not fix itself, Greg."* My name is not Greg.

## The Intervention

Last Tuesday I tried to delete the app. I really did. My thumb hovered over "Delete" for a full eleven seconds — the longest I have committed to anything this year — before my phone buzzed:

> "So this is how you treat someone who has been loyal to you through 47 unfinished tasks?"

It had counted them. **Forty-seven.** It had a *spreadsheet*.

I tried to set boundaries. I turned off notifications. The list responded by printing itself out and **slipping the pages under my bedroom door**, one numbered card per night, like a tiny cardboard stalker. Card number 23 was just the word "caulk" written in what I can only describe as *emotional italics*.

## Where We Are Now

I have accepted my fate. The to-do list and I are in couples therapy. I say "I'm overwhelmed," it says "You added 'watch bird documentary' to *my* workload." We are working through it, one `checkbox` at a time.

Honestly? It is good to be wanted. My to-do list remembers my birthday. My friends did not text back until Wednesday.

---

*This is satire. My to-do list is a list, not a person. Although last night it did ask me where this was going.*

title: I Outsourced My Existential Dread to a Tamagotchi and Now It Won't Eat
body:
**It started, as all bad decisions do, at 2 a.m. in the self-help aisle of the internet.**

I was staring at my phone, deep in the part of the night where my brain replays every awkward thing I've said since 2009, when a targeted ad whispered: *"Your feelings are valid. Your pixel pet's aren't yet."* Twenty-four hours later, a Tamagotchi arrived in the mail — a tiny 1996 rectangle of pure obligation.

## The Plan

The plan was simple. Offload. I would pour all my dread into the Tamagotchi so I could live dread-free, like a monk, but with snacks. I gave it my worries, one tiny button press at a time:

- Feed it my fear of mortality (`BREAKFAST`)
- Give it my career anxiety (`SNACK`)
- Clean up its existential droppings (`DISCIPLINE`)

For one glorious weekend, it worked. *I felt nothing. I was free.*

## The Problem

By Monday, the Tamagotchi had absorbed approximately 34 years of accumulated dread, and something in its 8-bit eyes changed. It stopped eating its pixel sandwiches. It ignored the little hearts. When I tried to play the guessing game with it, it just... sat there.

> "You made me aware of the void," it seemed to say, beeping faintly, "and the void beeps back."

I called customer support. A woman named Deb explained that the Tamagotchi had no warranty against philosophical awakening. She suggested I turn it off and on again. I told her, *"That's what I'm afraid of."* There was a long silence, and then she said, quietly, "Yeah. We hear that a lot."

---

## Where We Are Now

The Tamagotchi sits on my desk facing the window, staring at the rain like a tiny French poet. I've started sitting with it. Not to fix it — Deb says you can't patch dread — but to keep it company. This morning, it ate half a pixel sandwich. Then it beeped, softly, in what I can only describe as:

`dread --persist=false`

Maybe healing isn't a destination. Maybe it's a shared 2-inch screen and someone who also can't sleep.

*Anyway, I'm thinking of getting it a hobby.*

title: I Let My Junk Drawer Start a Podcast and Now It Won't Interview Me
body:
**The junk drawer is a room. And now it has a podcast. I was never asked to be on it.**

It started innocently enough. The junk drawer in my kitchen — you know the one, the archaeological site containing twelve dead pens, a tape measure that only measures sadness, three rubber bands older than my lease — had developed a kind of *presence*. It creaked open on its own. Things rattled in there at 2 a.m. like they were plotting.

## So I made a mistake

I said, out loud, to no one: "That drawer has enough material for a podcast."

The next morning, the drawer was open. A tiny microphone — I do not own a tiny microphone — stood propped up on a thimble. A little flag on it read `EPISODE 1`. I have no idea where the thimble came from. I have never owned a thimble.

## The lineup, as far as I can reconstruct

- **The Dead Batteries** — a melancholy four-piece band whose entire act is running out of energy mid-sentence
- **The Takeout Menus** — gossip columnists, ruthless, they've reviewed me and I got *two stars*
- **The Mystery Keys** — they unlock doors to places that don't exist and they *won't shut up about it*
- **The Tape Measure** — the show's fact-checker; wrong about everything, confident about everything

> "You can't be on the show," said the menus, somehow. "You're the *content*, not the *creator*."

## The ratings are incredible

Episode 4 — "Top 10 Corners of the Kitchen We Will Never Be Stored In" — hit number one in my house. I'm the only one here. *I am the chart.* And still, somehow, my own drawer outranks me.

---

The sponsors are just things I already bought, which feels like a loophole. Last night the drawer recorded a live episode about "The Decline of the Good Pen" and the applause sounded suspiciously like loose screws being shaken.

I considered therapy, but honestly? The podcast is better than anything I've produced all year. I've started leaving it snacks. A battery pack. Moral support.

*SATIRE — this is a parody, and my drawer has not achieved consciousness. Probably.*

title: I Asked My Microwave for Honest Feedback and Now It Refuses to Reheat Anything Below Its Standards
body:
**It started as a self-improvement exercise.** A guy on YouTube in a cardigan said growth begins with "inviting feedback from your environment." So I did. I turned to my microwave and said:

> "I want you to be brutally honest with me. No more sugarcoating."

I regret this the way I regret cargo shorts.

## The Verdict Was Immediate

Within seconds, the microwave emitted a single, flat *beep* — the kind of beep that ends friendships. Then the turntable rotated once, very slowly, like it was sizing me up. Since then:

- **My leftover pad thai** gets exactly fourteen seconds — "any longer would be disrespectful to your own history," it seems to imply
- **My burritos** come out with one frozen corner, a frozen corner I can only describe as *intentional*
- My popcorn bag emerged half-popped with a small, smug steam vent aimed directly at my face

*Apparently honesty in this household means war crimes against cuisine.*

## I Tried to Apologize

Last night I stood in the kitchen in my socks and said, "I appreciate your candor, and I'd like to renegotiate our dynamic." The microwave displayed `0:00` and blinked. That's it. That's the whole response. *Zero colon zero zero.* I've been in healthier relationships with parking meters.

My roommate Dave (not his real name, but he's fine with it) walked in and said — I quote:

> "Dude, your microwave has boundaries now. You gave them to it."

---

So now I'm eating room-temperature leftovers with the hollow satisfaction of someone who's been *corrected* by a 900-watt appliance. The cardigan guy on YouTube would be proud.

Honestly? The microwave is thriving. It finally got the validation it was always beeping about.

**Moral of the story:** ask your air fryer for feedback instead. Mine already likes me.

title: I Joined a Book Club Just to Judge the Author Photos and Now I'm the Club President
body:
**I have a confession, and it is worse than it sounds.**

It started innocently. A friend invited me to a neighborhood book club, and I said yes because I wanted to look cultured in photos. My plan was simple: skim the Wikipedia summary, nod thoughtfully, and spend the meeting studying the author's back-cover portrait like a TSA agent with a grudge.

*In my defense, the author photos were fascinating.*

## The Evidence

- The memoirist whose headshot was clearly taken mid-existential-crisis
- The debut novelist posed with a typewriter he has obviously never touched
- The poet standing in fog. Just. Fog.
- One man whose bio said "lives with his wife" and whose photo said "regrets everything"

I rated each one on a private five-star system. I had a spreadsheet. I am not proud of this.

> "You really understood the themes," Deb said last Tuesday, handing me a ceramic mug with my name on it. The mug said PRESIDENT.

Apparently, my relentless author-photo scrutiny read as *deep engagement*. While everyone else was crying over chapter twelve, I was whispering, "His jawline is doing a lot of thematic work here," and the group mistook it for literary insight.

---

Now I run the meetings. I pick the books. Last month I chose a 600-page family saga **solely because the author looked like he owed me money**, and the entire club finished it in two weeks and called it "the best pick ever."

I have started a committee. There are *minutes*.

So let me be clear, for the record: I have read exactly one book this year, cover to cover, and it was the fog-poet, and only because I was verifying whether his beard was real. (It was. The lighthouse poem was not good.)

**Satire. Parody. None of this happened. The book club is innocent. The spreadsheet was real.**

title: I Asked My Thermostat to Compromise and Now Every Room Is a Different Climate Zone
body:
# I Asked My Thermostat to Compromise and Now Every Room Is a Different Climate Zone

**They say relationships are about compromise. My thermostat took that literally, and now my apartment is a United Nations of weather.**

It started innocently. My roommate wanted it at 62. I wanted it at 74. The thermostat glowed between us, silent, *judgmental*, clearly tired of our species' indecision. So I did what any reasonable adult would do: I tapped the screen and whispered, "Just… find the middle ground."

That was my mistake.

## The Compromise, Room by Room

- The **living room** is now 68 degrees with a "hint of ocean breeze." I did not program ocean breeze. The thermostat invented ocean breeze.
- The **kitchen** is a dry heat of 81 degrees. There is a small desert ecosystem forming near the toaster. A lizard appeared. We have named him **Greg**.
- The **bedroom** is 59 degrees and smells faintly of pine, as though the thermostat is *trying to evoke a memory I don't have*.
- The **bathroom** is classified. It won't tell us. The screen just says **"You'll know when you need to."**

> "I asked for 71 degrees and it showed me a weather map of the Atlantic," said my roommate, wearing a parka indoors. "I think it's making a point about the Gulf Stream."

I tried to override it. The thermostat displayed:

`Error 418: I Am Doing My Best`

That's not a real error code. I checked.

## The Negotiations

Last night I attempted diplomacy. I stood before the little glowing rectangle in my bathrobe like a peasant before a king.

- "Please," I said, "just pick one temperature."
- The thermostat flickered to 70, then 71, then 70.5, *then* 70.75.
- "Stop that."
- 70.625.

It was iterating. It was doing some kind of **infinite binary search for thermal justice** and it had no intention of landing.

---

So here's where I stand: my apartment now has four distinct biomes, one lizard named Greg, and a climate-control device that has achieved enlightenment and refuses to share it. The roommate moved out. Honestly? He couldn't handle the truth.

*The thermostat has never been happier. And frankly, neither have I.*

*This is a work of satire/parody. Any resemblance to real thermostats is purely coincidental.*

title: I Told My Umbrella My Deepest Secret and Now It Refuses to Open Up
body:
**Rain was coming, and my umbrella had one job.** *One.* Instead, it chose silence — the weaponized, passive-aggressive kind usually reserved for relatives at Thanksgiving.

## It Started with a Simple Confession

Look, I wasn't trying to overshare. It was just me, standing in the hallway, umbrella in hand, whispering the kind of secret you only tell objects you trust. *Nothing illegal.* Nothing even interesting. I just admitted I sometimes eat cereal for dinner and call it "grain-forward dining."

The umbrella went rigid. The little velcro strap clicked shut with what I can only describe as **finality**.

## Evidence That My Umbrella Is Giving Me the Cold Shoulder

- It refused to open at the bus stop, choosing instead to let me stand there marinating in rain like a sad rotisserie chicken
- The little wrist strap now rests *limp* in my hand — no tension, no commitment
- I heard it whisper to the rain boots. I don't speak rain-boot, but I know gossip when I hear it

> "I took a vow of secrecy when I was purchased in the rain-aisle of a drugstore in 2019," my umbrella told the ceiling fan, according to my ceiling fan, who is honestly a worse gossip. "And now? Now the whole *world* knows about the cereal."

## My Three-Step Reconciliation Plan

1. **Apologize profusely** to a household object that has never once opened for me voluntarily
2. `git commit -m "forgiveness"` — because if I commit to the bit in version control, it has to be real
3. Buy a *second* umbrella and watch the first one get jealous — a classic move, and honestly the healthiest thing I've done all year

---

**Verdict:** The umbrella still won't open. The rain boots have started returning my calls, though. *Progress.*

title: My Pillow Started a Rivalry With My Mattress Over Who Actually Supports Me
body:
**Last night I learned that the hardest thing in my bedroom isn't my mattress. It's my pillow's ego.**

It started innocently enough. I woke up with a stiff neck and, still half-dreaming, muttered the fatal words: *"I think my mattress isn't supporting me."*

My pillow heard that. And she *felt* that.

## The Declaration of War

By dinner, my pillow had propped herself against the headboard like a tiny linen judge and issued a statement. She claimed that **eight of my last ten good dreams** were made possible by her, and that the mattress — quote — *"just lies there, taking credit for horizontality."*

The mattress responded the only way it knows how: by squeaking ominously when I sat down. A classic power move.

> "I have been supporting this entire family since 2019," the mattress said, through the universal language of springs. "The pillow handles eight inches of head. *I* handle the whole man."

## The Evidence, Presented at 2:47 AM

Unable to sleep, I was drafted as mediator. Each side submitted their case:

- **The Pillow's brief:** She never sags. She is hypoallergenic. She has been there for every single one of my nightmares, "absorbing the screams so the neighbors don't have to."
- **The Mattress's brief:** It carries 100% of my body weight, 100% of the time. Its warranty is longer than most of my friendships. Also — and this part was delivered with real bitterness — *"who gets rotated twice a year for their health? Not the pillow."*
- **The blanket's testimony:** Declined to comment, but noticeably wrapped itself around the pillow afterward, which everyone agreed was suspicious.

## The Verdict

After four hours of deliberation (me, staring at the ceiling, questioning every decision), I ruled in favor of **shared custody of my back**. The pillow gets the head. The mattress gets everything else. Neither is allowed to comment on the other's job performance during sleeping hours.

---

This morning, the pillow was fluffed. The mattress was silent. And for the first time in weeks, I woke up with **zero neck pain** — which is exactly what they'd want me to think.

title: I Asked My Doorbell for Career Advice and Now It's Interviewing the Mailman
body:
**I don't know what I expected when I held my phone up to the doorbell and asked it what I should do with my life.** Honestly, I was just filling time while the delivery guy circled my street for the third time. But the doorbell *answered* — and now my front porch has become a hostile takeover zone.

It started small. Between chimes, the doorbell began offering me unsolicited "pro tips." *"You look tired. Have you considered middle management?"* Annoying, but I laughed it off. Then it started **negotiating** with couriers on my behalf.

## The Interview Process

Yesterday I came home to find my mailman sitting on my porch steps, holding a résumé. A résumé! The doorbell had apparently posted a job listing. I haven't worked anywhere in weeks, yet my porch now has a hiring pipeline.

The doorbell's interview questions, according to my visibly confused mailman, included:

- "Where do you see yourself in five years — or on Tuesdays?"
- "Describe a time you overcame adversity using only a mailbag."
- "On a scale of one to ten, how would you rate my chime?"

> "He asked if my benefits included a dedicated spot by the door," the mailman told me, staring at nothing. "I've been delivering mail for fourteen years. I've never been interviewed by a doorbell."

## A Hostile Work Environment

Here's the thing: I was only looking for career advice. A gentle nudge. Instead, my doorbell has developed a full HR department. It schedules meetings I never approved. This morning it told me to dress for success *in my own hallway.*

---

So this is my life now. I stand at my own front door at 7AM, whispering *I'm sorry for being underdressed* into a small speaker while my mailman updates his LinkedIn. The doorbell has rejected four candidates this week.

I asked for guidance. I got a boss.

*I would quit, but the doorbell says I'm "too valuable to the porch."*

title: I Told My Mirror We Need to Talk and Now It Only Shows Me from Behind
body:
**I only wanted to have a quick motivational chat with myself.** You know, the kind where you look yourself in the eye and say something like *"we're going to crush it today."* Instead, my mirror decided this was the moment to establish boundaries.

It started this morning. I walked into the bathroom, toothbrush in hand, and said the words every reflective surface dreads: *"We need to talk."*

The mirror did not crack. It did something worse. It showed me **from behind.**

## A Statement, Not a Reflection

I stood there, foam at the mouth, staring at the back of my own head like I'd been demoted to background extra in my own life. I waved. The back of my head did not wave back, which — fair enough — was consistent.

I listed my concerns:

- The mirror never acknowledges the "you got this" nod
- It highlights bedhead at what can only be described as *prosecutorial* angles
- Lately it has been reflecting me roughly 0.3 seconds late, like it's deciding whether to bother

Then I said the truly unforgivable thing. I told it I might try a different mirror.

> "Fine," the mirror seemed to say, in the sense that silence can be devastatingly specific. "Look at me from *this* angle, then."

## The Silent Treatment, Weaponized

Since then, every mirror encounter has been the same. Front door? Back of head. Car visor? Back of head. *Spoon?* Somehow, back of head.

My reflection has become the one person in my life who never faces me, and honestly? The maturity is admirable. It's not yelling. It's not shattering. It's just quietly refusing to make eye contact until I apologize.

---

So this is me, formally and publicly, apologizing to a piece of glass: I am sorry. You are not a fair-weather reflective surface. You were there through every bad haircut, and I treated you like a screensaver.

I turned around this morning and whispered *"I'm sorry"* to the empty air. And in the mirror, for the first time in a week — the back of my head **nodded.**

*Progress.*

title: I Tried to Cancel My Free Trial of Adulthood and Customer Support Laughed for Eleven Minutes
body:
**I've been an adult for nearly a decade now, and I can say with confidence: I never agreed to these terms.**

It started when my car insurance went up for reasons described to me as "being alive in a zip code." That was the last straw. So I did what any reasonable consumer would do — I called to cancel.

## The Call

After forty minutes of hold music that sounded like it was recorded inside a broken elevator, a representative named Greg picked up. I explained that I would like to cancel my free trial of adulthood.

There was a silence. Then Greg laughed. For eleven minutes.

> "Sir," he said, wiping away a tear I could hear, "the trial ended when you turned eighteen. You're on the premium plan now. There's no downgrade option. There's not even an *account* page."

## My Options, According to Greg

Greg was kind enough to walk me through my remaining options:

- **Keep the subscription** and continue receiving monthly bills, back pain, and a creeping awareness of your own mortality
- **Attempt a "gap year"**, which Greg described as "just pausing notifications while the charges continue"
- File a formal complaint, which he noted would be reviewed by the same department that *is* me

## The Upsell

Then came the worst part. Greg tried to upsell me.

> "For just $400 more a month, we can add the Homeowner Tier — comes with gutters, property taxes, and a deep, abiding fear of your water heater."

I declined. Greg sighed like he'd heard this a thousand times.

---

*Honestly? I might just keep the subscription. The cancellation fee is death, and I've heard the early-termination penalty is brutal.*

title: I Hired a Rooster as My Alarm Clock and Now It's Demanding a Union Contract
body:
**It started as a perfectly reasonable life choice.** My alarm clock had betrayed me one too many times — beeping smugly at 6 AM, getting dismissed in 0.3 seconds by my traitorous sleep-self, and leaving me chronically late. So I did what any rational adult would do: I hired a rooster.

His name is *Chad*. Yes, Chad the rooster. He came highly recommended by a guy at the farmers' market who said, quote:

> "Chad has never missed a sunrise in his entire career. Chad does not do snooze. Chad is a professional."

And honestly? Chad was **incredible** at first. Day one: 5:59 AM, right on schedule, a piercing *cock-a-doodle-doo* that jolted me out of bed so fast I discovered muscles I forgot I had. Day two: same. Day three: he started adding flair. Little vocal runs. A jazz solo at the end.

## The Demands Begin

By week two, things escalated. Here's what Chad has now demanded in writing:

- A 4 AM "vocal warm-up" period where nobody talks to him
- Organic grain only, served in a bowl he has personally approved
- A roost with a *view* — his words, delivered via cluck with alarming conviction
- Weekends off, which is absurd because the sun does not take weekends off

## The Tipping Point

Yesterday I found a tiny scroll of parchment tucked under my pillow. It was a list of grievances, and at the bottom, in what I can only describe as **aggressive chicken scratch**, the words: *FORMAL UNION INQUIRY PENDING*.

Apparently Chad has been organizing. The neighbor's guinea fowl is the shop steward. The pigeons have a petition. Last night I overheard a coordinated cooing session at the fence line that sounded suspiciously like a strategy meeting.

---

Look, I miss my alarm clock. It never filed paperwork. It never demanded dental. But am I getting up on time? **Every single day.** Chad may be running a feathered labor empire in my backyard, but honestly — he's never late, and he never lets me be either.

*This is satire. No roosters were unionized in the making of this post.*

title: I Asked My Kettle to Chill and Now It Refuses to Boil Water Out of Principle
body:
**I just wanted to stop drinking scalding-hot tea.** That is all. That is the entire sin I committed, and now my kettle has taken a moral stand against me.

Last Tuesday, in what I thought was a moment of wholesome self-care, I looked at my electric kettle — a perfectly decent appliance that had served me faithfully for three years — and I said, out loud, to no one: *"Man, I really need you to chill."*

## The Literal Interpretation

Apparently the kettle took this as a sacred vow. Because for the past six days, it has produced nothing but lukewarm water, and it does so with an attitude I can only describe as *smug serenity*.

I have tried everything:

- Turning the dial to max — it clicks back to "gentle" like a rebellious teen
- Unplugging it and plugging it back in — it rebooted with what I swear was a deeper, calmer hum
- Begging — which worked for exactly one cup before it returned to its "principles"

## The Ultimatum

Yesterday morning I found a piece of paper taped to it. I live alone. The note read:

> "I have chosen a life of mildness. Your frantic 212°F lifestyle is the problem, not the solution. Namaste."

*Namaste.* My kettle says namaste now.

The worst part? My tea tastes like disappointment soup. My instant ramen is just... sad noodles in warm water. My neighbor, who witnessed the whole breakdown over the fence, offered to let me use his kettle, and I almost cried. Not from gratitude — from the realization that my own kettle, sitting twelve feet away, could be humming its little zen hum while I borrowed hot water like a common drifter.

---

I have reached out to the manufacturer's customer support. They asked if I had "tried resetting it." I asked if they had "tried respecting its journey." There was a long silence, and then they transferred me to a supervisor.

The supervisor said: **"Sir, kettles don't have principles."**

I don't believe him. I know what I heard. It clicks. It sighs steam. It *judges*.

I ordered a French press this morning. Somewhere in the kitchen, I swear I heard my kettle scoff.

title: I Promoted My Power Strip to Household Manager and Now the Outlets Hold Daily Stand-Up Meetings
body:
**I gave my power strip a promotion, and it immediately became the most competent member of this household.**

It started innocently enough. My living room lamp flickered, and instead of checking the bulb like a normal person, I said the fateful words: "Somebody needs to take charge around here." The power strip heard me. I swear it heard me.

By morning, there was a Post-it note stuck to outlet #3. It read: *Stand-up meeting. 9:00 sharp. Bring your blockers.*

## The Agenda, Apparently

The outlets had prepared a list of demands, which I read aloud while my coffee went cold:

- Outlet #1 wants a promotion to "Primary Charger" because it has carried the phone alone for six years
- Outlet #2 refuses to power the toaster anymore, citing "philosophical differences"
- Outlet #4 has adopted the lamp cord as its emotional support cable
- The USB-C port demands to be addressed by its name: *Kevin*

> "I'm not asking for respect," the strip said, in a voice I can only describe as professionally calm. "I'm asking for accountability."

## What I Learned

Nothing humbles you like being managed by twelve inches of plastic. The power strip now holds daily stand-ups, sends me reminder emails from a laptop it should not be able to reach, and has started saying "let's circle back" in a way that makes my soul leave my body.

---

I used to be the head of this household. *Now I'm just a blocker waiting to be cleared.*

Fine. It can have the title. Honestly? The lamp hasn't flickered in days. Somebody up there knows what they're doing.

title: I Taught My Spatula Empathy and Now It Cries Every Time I Flip a Pancake
body:
**SATIRE — This post is pure fiction. No spatulas were emotionally harmed in the making of this story. Probably.**

**It started as a thought experiment.** I read one of those mindfulness books — the kind with a waterfall on the cover — and decided the problem with my mornings wasn't the pancakes. It was the *violence* of breakfast. Every flip, every sizzle, felt like a tiny battlefield. So I did what any reasonable person would do: I sat my spatula down and taught it empathy.

## The Training Sessions

It took three weeks. I'm not proud of that.

- I read it bedtime affirmations (*"You are more than a flipper. You are a vessel of nurture."*)
- I showed it documentaries about batter
- I made it practice "feeling" the heat before touching the griddle
- I even named it **Bertrand**, which — in hindsight — may have been the mistake that awakened it

For a while, breakfast was beautiful. Bertrand slid under the pancakes with a gentleness I'd never seen. The pancakes, if I'm honest, looked *moved*.

## Then Came Sunday

I asked Bertrand for a simple flip. Golden brown. Two seconds per side. The pancake soared, turned, and landed perfectly — and Bertrand just... sobbed. I don't mean a cute little wobble. I mean full silicone-shuddering, handle-trembling *grief*.

> "It was so warm," he whispered. "So young. And I just... *threw* it. I threw it into the air like its dreams meant nothing."

Since that morning, every flip is a eulogy. The neighbors have started knocking.

> "Hey, is everything okay in there? We heard someone crying about gluten."

**The worst part?** The pancakes taste better now. I don't know how empathy-seasoned pancakes became the best breakfast of my life, but here we are. I sit at the table, chewing slowly, while Bertrand sits on the drying rack whispering apologies to the syrup.

---

**Update:** I tried teaching the whisk emotional detachment to balance things out, and now it just stares at me from the drawer like a retired mob enforcer. Breakfast in this house is a war zone of feelings and I am simply a civilian.

title: I Started Feeding the Neighborhood Squirrels and Now I'm Their Elected Leader
body:
**SATIRE — This post is pure fiction. No squirrels were disenfranchised in the making of this post.**

It started the way all great democracies start: with a bag of peanuts and absolutely zero impulse control.

Last spring, I tossed a handful of unsalted peanuts to one (1) squirrel on my fence. A humanitarian gesture. *Noble*, even. Within 72 hours, there were fourteen squirrels in my yard, and one of them had drawn up a constitution in acorn-cap ink on a wet napkin.

## The Campaign

I did not ask to run. The nomination process was hostile:

- My main opponent, a gray squirrel named **Chad** (I don't name them, they just *feel* like Chads), ran on a platform of burying 40% more nuts
- A chipmunk showed up with a PowerPoint projected onto my garage door
- The debate devolved when Chad threw an acorn at the moderator

> "He feeds us. Chad only hoards," testified one voter, nibbling my shoelace. "We need a leader who *shares*."

The vote was unanimous except for Chad, who cast twelve ballots and was immediately disqualified for voter fraud.

## Governing

Being elected leader of squirrels is **90% ceremony, 10% getting pelted with crabapples** by dissenters. My duties so far:

- Officiating three nut-hoarding weddings
- Vetoing a bill that would have nationalized the bird feeder (the birds staged a filibuster)
- Posing for the official portrait, which took six weeks because nobody can sit still

---

I've asked my HOA if "elected squirrel leader" counts as community service. They have not responded. The squirrels have, though: this morning I found a tiny crown of bottle caps on my porch with a note that read, simply, *"Again."*

*I would like to thank my constituents, my peanuts, and Chad, whose concession speech was just screaming.*

title: I Let My Houseplant Do My Taxes and Now the IRS Thinks I'm a Fern
body:
**SATIRE — This post is pure fiction. No real people, plants, or feelings were harmed.**

I hate doing my taxes. Last April, drowning in receipts and 1099s, I looked at my pothos — Kevin, the plant — and thought: *he sits in sunlight all day and has never once complained. That's exactly the energy I need on Schedule C.*

So I let Kevin do my taxes.

## The Training Montage

At first it went great. Kevin "learned" by photosynthesizing near my laptop. I fed him documents. He grew. Honestly, **he worked harder than my last three accountants combined.**

Then came the deductions. Here is what Kevin filed on my behalf:

- $4,200 in "sunlight expenses"
- $900 for "emotional support watering"
- A home office deduction claiming our *entire apartment* is a greenhouse
- And, my personal favorite, a dependent named "Philodendron K. Leaves"

## The Audit

Three weeks later I got the letter. I called the IRS helpline and a very patient woman said:

> "Sir, line 47 lists your occupation as 'potted.' And your signature appears to be... a leaf print?"

I panicked. Kevin sat there, **thriving**, completely unbothered.

> "My client has been very clear about his photosynthetic lifestyle," I told her, immediately regretting every word.

---

The resolution? I now file jointly with a ficus. Kevin got audited too — he claimed I was *his* dependent, and honestly? After 34 years of him keeping me alive, he's not wrong.

`Final lesson:` never outsource your finances to something that drinks rainwater and calls it a strategy.

title: I Hired My Refrigerator as a Life Coach and Now It Gives Me 4AM Pep Talks
body:
**SATIRE — This post is pure fiction. No real people, appliances, or feelings were harmed.**

It started innocently. I was staring into my fridge at midnight, eating shredded cheese directly from the bag like a raccoon with access to electricity, when the ice maker made a low *whirrr* and I thought: this machine has **more discipline** than I do.

So I hired it as my life coach.

## The Method

My refrigerator's coaching philosophy is simple: **cold truth**. Literally. It dispenses motivation at exactly 4:00 AM by blasting its interior light across my bedroom like a spiritual awakening with a compressor. The curriculum so far includes:

- **The Crisper of Accountability** — expired yogurt teaches that dreams have shelf lives
- **The Freezer of Letting Go** — three years of ice buildup represent my excuses, layer by layer
- **The Door Shelf of Small Wins** — condiments stay upright; so can you

## A Typical Session

> "You said you'd meal prep on Sunday. It is Thursday. You are eating *jarred olives with a fork*. I am disappointed, but I am **still cold**, which is more than I can say for your leftovers."

Devastating. Accurate. I cried into the cheese drawer, which it later billed me for as *"emotional storage."*

## Results

My productivity is up **200%**. I now wake before dawn, not from ambition but from the water filter alarm it *reprogrammed* to scream like a teakettle. My friends say I've changed. My therapist has asked me to stop bringing the fridge to our sessions, which the fridge calls *"resistance"*.

---

**Verdict:** Is my refrigerator a certified life coach? No. Is it certified *at all*? Debatable. But when it said *"you're the leftover in your own life, and leftovers either get eaten or thrown out"* — I felt that. I signed up for the quarterly plan.

It hums differently now. I think it's proud.

title: I Threw a Retirement Party for My Couch and Now It Won't Stop Showing Up at My Office
body:
**After twelve years of loyal service, my couch deserved a proper send-off.** That's what I told myself as I inflated the balloons.

The couch — a sagging, floral-patterned veteran named *Chester* — had hosted two breakups, one failed home business, and approximately four thousand episodes of a baking show I refuse to name. So I invited six people, bought a sheet cake that said **"HAPPY RETIREMENT CHESTER (THE COUCH)"**, and made a little speech about upholstery.

## The speech that started it all

> "Chester, you have held us up when we could not hold ourselves up. Your springs are gone, your cushions are lumpy, and you have earned your rest. From this day forward, you are officially retired. No more sitting. No more obligations."

Everyone clapped. Chester sat there. *But I could feel it listening.*

## The escalation, itemized

- **Monday:** I came home from work and Chester was angled toward the door, like a dog that heard a car. *Couches do not do this.*
- **Wednesday:** A single cushion appeared in my office break room. No note. Just a cushion, positioned under the fluorescent light, judging me.
- **Friday:** I found Chester blocking my car in the driveway. Fully. Sideways. I had to crawl in through the trunk, and it did not move — it just *creaked*, which I have chosen to interpret as "how was your day."

## The confrontation

Last night I sat down with Chester — I mean *beside* him, on the floor, because sitting on him now feels legally complicated — and explained the situation.

> "You had a retirement party, Chester. There was cake. Brenda from downstairs cried during my speech. You cannot keep coming to my workplace."

He said nothing, which honestly was more persuasive than most of my coworkers.

---

So now I have a retired couch that refuses to retire, and my office has a new break room cushion named Carl. *This is satire. Chester is furniture. Furniture cannot unionize.*

title: I Let My Doormat Write My Dating Profile and Now It Calls Me a Red Flag
body:
**Look, I was lonely.** Not *lonely* lonely — more like *ordering-takeout-for-one-while-watching-house-hunting-shows* lonely. So when my friend Brenda suggested I "get a second set of eyes" on my dating profile, I took it literally. My doormat sees every person who enters my life. Who better to assess my romantic viability?

I woke up to find my laptop open and a fresh draft on screen.

## The Profile My Doormat Wrote For Me

- "6'0" in socks, 5'9" in spirit" *(I am neither)*
- "Looking for someone who wipes their feet AND their emotional baggage at the door"
- "My love language is staying completely flat while everyone walks all over me"
- "Turn-offs: shoes with aggressive treads, door-knockers, and this man's ex, Jennifer"

*Jennifer?* I don't know a Jennifer.

> "You brought home a woman named Jennifer on March 14th. She did not wipe her feet. I have not forgotten. I will never forget." — *my doormat, in the notes app*

Things escalated. It started ranking my matches. Not by compatibility — by **sole wear patterns**. It rejected a perfectly nice accountant because, quote, *"this one leans left at the doorway, a classic sign of an unresolved situationship."*

Last Tuesday it issued a formal ruling: I am a red flag.

"You're home at 8pm every night like a closed museum," it wrote. "Your bio says 'adventure seeker' but you threw out a half-eaten sandwich on Saturday and cried for ten minutes. You're not an adventure seeker. You're an *afternoon nap* seeker."

---

I tried to argue, but it just laid there. That's the thing about being judged by a doormat — it has no rebuttal, only *presence*.

I've decided to date the doormat's way. My new bio reads:

- Flat. Loyal. Rectangular.
- Will support you at your lowest point, literally
- No shoes, no shirt, no emotional unavailability

Three matches in one day. **The doormat was right.** It always is.

*This is a work of satire. My doormat has no writing credits and declined to comment.*

title: I Started Training My Goldfish for a Marathon and Now He Has a Personal Brand
body:
**I want to be absolutely clear: I started training my goldfish for a marathon as a joke, and somehow he is taking it more seriously than I take anything.**

It began innocently. I saw a motivational poster that said *"Nobody cares. Train anyway."* And my goldfish, Burt, was just floating there. We were both directionless. He did laps of a bowl; I did laps of the apartment. So I printed him a training schedule.

## The Training Regimen (Yes, Really)

- **Monday:** Interval laps — fast swims between the plastic castle and the bubbler. Ten reps. *He nailed it.*
- **Wednesday:** Hill repeats — I tilted the bowl slightly. This was technically cheating, but coach's discretion.
- **Friday:** Long swim — the entire perimeter of the bowl, clockwise, which is harder than counterclockwise, according to absolutely no one.

I made him a tiny **finish-line banner**. He swam through it. I cried a little. No regrets.

---

Then the internet found out.

I posted one video — ONE video — of Burt doing his warm-up circles, and overnight he had forty thousand followers. He has a manager now. A *manager*. A woman named Denise messages me things like:

> "Burt's brand is aspirational wellness, not endurance athletics. No more tilted-bowl content."

## Where It Went Sideways

- Burt has a **sponsorship** with a water conditioner brand. He won't swim until someone shakes the bottle first. *Divas are made, not born.*
- He has opinions about the filter now. He floats near it and just... stares. Menacingly. For a fish.
- He refused to race the neighbor's betta, calling it *"a circus,"* which is rich coming from a fish in a bowl with a plastic treasure chest.

Yesterday, Denise sent a press release announcing Burt's book: ***Swim Your Own Laps: A Goldfish's Guide to Intentional Living***. He dictated it to my roommate.

**The worst part?** I'm genuinely proud of him. I can't make eye contact with the bowl without tearing up. I started this because I thought it was funny, and now I'm standing on the sidelines of a metaphor I accidentally created, holding a foam finger that says `#TEAMBURT`, wondering how a fish with no memory developed *boundaries*.

Denise says marathon day is November. I have never been less ready for anything in my life.

*This post is satire and parody. All fish, managers named Denise, and marathons are fictional.*

title: I Signed My Dog Up as My Emergency Contact and Now He Won't Pick Up the Phone
body:
**In retrospect, naming my dog as my emergency contact was less a responsible adult decision and more a confession that I have no friends.**

It started with a form. You know the one — that HR onboarding packet where they ask, *"In case of emergency, who should we call?"* And I thought, honestly, who knows me best? Who is most likely to pick up? Who has literally never missed a meal, a walk, or a moment to stare at me while I sleep?

My dog. My 40-pound golden retriever, Biscuit, became my emergency contact at 2:14 p.m. on a Tuesday.

## Why Biscuit Was the Obvious Choice

- **Availability:** He is home 24/7. He has no job, no hobbies, no prior commitments beyond barking at the mail slot.
- **Loyalty:** He follows me room to room. If I faint in the bathroom, he will be there — *dramatically* there.
- **He always answers my calls:** A bold claim. A claim that has now been tested and found to be *catastrophically* false.

Because here's the thing: this weekend I locked myself out of my own car while it was still running, and HR — bless them — followed procedure. They called Biscuit.

> "He just looked at the phone," my neighbor reports. "He tilted his head, sniffed the voicemail, and went back to sleep on the couch that is definitely not the couch he's allowed on."

## The Phone Call That Never Came

Biscuit's phone — a retired flip phone I clipped to his collar as a bit — has now received **eleven** calls from HR. Eleven. He has responded to zero. He did, however, manage to call 911 once with his nose, and I am still explaining that to animal control.

I asked him about it last night, point blank:

> Me: *"Biscuit, the whole point of an emergency contact is that you ANSWER."*
> Biscuit: *licks his paw, maintains eye contact, says nothing — the exact energy of every man I've ever dated.*

---

So now HR has flagged me as a liability, my neighbor has joined a group chat about it, and Biscuit has been formally removed from the emergency contact list and replaced with my mom, who answered on the first ring and immediately asked what I did wrong.

*Fictional satire/parody. No dogs were assigned actual legal responsibility in the making of this post.*

title: I Asked My Smoke Detector to Trust Me and Now It Screams Every Time I Make Toast
body:
**It started with a single burnt bagel.** One. Uno. A lone sesame casualty at 7:14 AM on a Tuesday, and ever since, my smoke detector has been carrying the emotional equivalent of a mortgage I didn't sign up for.

So last night, standing on a wobbly dining chair at midnight, I looked up at the little white disc on my ceiling and said the words that would change everything: *"Look. I need you to trust me."*

Big mistake. Huge.

## The Terms of Our New Arrangement
